claim: The activation induced cytidine deaminase (AID) protein is known to initiate somatic hypermutation, gene conversion or switch recombination by cytidine deamination within the immunoglobulin loci.
source: The activation induced cytidine deaminase (AID) protein is known to initiate somatic hypermutation, gene conversion or switch recombination by cytidine deamination within the immunoglobulin loci.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about AID function in immunoglobulin diversification.

claim: AID leads to intra- and intergenic deletions via homologous recombination of sequence repeats.
source: Using chromosomally integrated fluorescence reporter transgenes, we demonstrate a new recombinogenic activity of AID leading to intra- and intergenic deletions via homologous recombination of sequence repeats.
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data using fluorescence reporter transgenes to demonstrate this activity.

claim: Repeat recombination occurs at high frequencies even when the homologous sequences are hundreds of bases away from the positions of AID-mediated cytidine deamination.
source: Repeat recombination occurs at high frequencies even when the homologous sequences are hundreds of bases away from the positions of AID-mediated cytidine deamination, suggesting DNA end resection before strand invasion.
evidence: This is based on experimental observations from the reporter constructs showing recombination at distant sites.

claim: Analysis of recombinants between homeologous repeats yielded evidence for heteroduplex formation.
source: Analysis of recombinants between homeologous repeats yielded evidence for heteroduplex formation and preferential migration of the Holliday junctions to the boundaries of sequence homology.
evidence: Sequence analysis of recombinants provided evidence for heteroduplex formation.

claim: Holliday junctions preferentially migrate to the boundaries of sequence homology.
source: Analysis of recombinants between homeologous repeats yielded evidence for heteroduplex formation and preferential migration of the Holliday junctions to the boundaries of sequence homology.
evidence: Sequence analysis of recombinants showed this preferential migration pattern.

claim: AID is essential for all types of B cell-specific immunoglobulin (Ig) gene diversification—somatic hypermutation (SH), gene conversion (GC), and class switch recombination (CSR).
source: The activation induced cytidine deaminase (AID) is essential for all types of B cell-specific immunoglobulin (Ig) gene diversification—somatic hypermutation (SH), gene conversion (GC), and class switch recombination (CSR) (Muramatsu et al., 2000; Revy et al., 2000; Arakawa et al., 2002; Harris et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: AID likely initiates immunoglobulin diversification processes by the deamination of deoxycytidines to uracils.
source: AID likely initiates these processes by the deamination of deoxycytidines to uracils, as inactivation of the DNA Uracil Glycosylase (UNG) gene changed the SH spectrum at C/G bases toward transitions and impaired GC and CSR (Di Noia and Neuberger, 2002; Rada et al., 2004; Saribasak et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by experimental evidence from UNG gene inactivation studies cited in the text.

claim: Inactivation of the DNA Uracil Glycosylase (UNG) gene changed the SH spectrum at C/G bases toward transitions and impaired GC and CSR.
source: AID likely initiates these processes by the deamination of deoxycytidines to uracils, as inactivation of the DNA Uracil Glycosylase (UNG) gene changed the SH spectrum at C/G bases toward transitions and impaired GC and CSR (Di Noia and Neuberger, 2002; Rada et al., 2004; Saribasak et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: Abasic sites resulting from the excision of AID-induced uracils are most likely removed by the apurinic/apyrimidinic endonuclease 1.
source: Abasic sites resulting from the excision of AID-induced uracils are most likely removed by the apurinic/apyrimidinic endonuclease 1 (Masani et al., 2013), but how the nicked DNA strands are further processed to initiate alternatively CSR, GC, or SH is poorly understood.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Masani et al., 2013.

claim: How the nicked DNA strands are further processed to initiate alternatively CSR, GC, or SH is poorly understood.
source: Abasic sites resulting from the excision of AID-induced uracils are most likely removed by the apurinic/apyrimidinic endonuclease 1 (Masani et al., 2013), but how the nicked DNA strands are further processed to initiate alternatively CSR, GC, or SH is poorly understood.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of scientific knowledge.

claim: AID-dependent double-strand breaks are believed to be generated by deamination of nearby cytidines on both strands of sequence repeats within switch regions.
source: AID-dependent double-strand breaks—believed to be generated by deamination of nearby cytidines on both strands of sequence repeats within switch regions—have been detected during CSR (Wuerffel et al., 1997; Petersen et al., 2001; Rush et al., 2004; Schrader et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies that detected these breaks during CSR.

claim: AID-dependent double-strand breaks have been detected during CSR.
source: AID-dependent double-strand breaks—believed to be generated by deamination of nearby cytidines on both strands of sequence repeats within switch regions—have been detected during CSR (Wuerffel et al., 1997; Petersen et al., 2001; Rush et al., 2004; Schrader et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to experimental studies.

claim: Double-strand breaks during CSR are normally joined by non-homologous end joining leading to the deletion of the intervening DNA sequence.
source: These breaks are normally joined by non-homologous end joining leading to the deletion of the intervening DNA sequence, but erroneous repair may lead to chromosomal translocations (reviewed by Boboila et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a review article.

claim: Erroneous repair of double-strand breaks during CSR may lead to chromosomal translocations.
source: These breaks are normally joined by non-homologous end joining leading to the deletion of the intervening DNA sequence, but erroneous repair may lead to chromosomal translocations (reviewed by Boboila et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a review article.

claim: It is uncertain whether double-strand breaks routinely accompany somatic hypermutation.
source: It is uncertain, however, whether double-strand breaks routinely accompany SH, since breaks within hypermutating V segments were subsequently found to be AID independent (Papavasiliou and Schatz, 2002; Bross and Jacobs, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations showing that breaks in V segments were AID independent.

claim: Breaks within hypermutating V segments were found to be AID independent.
source: It is uncertain, however, whether double-strand breaks routinely accompany SH, since breaks within hypermutating V segments were subsequently found to be AID independent (Papavasiliou and Schatz, 2002; Bross and Jacobs, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: It remains unclear whether gene conversion is initiated by a double strand-break or by a single-strand nick.
source: Similarly, it remains unclear whether GC is initiated by a double strand-break or by a single-strand nick (Yabuki et al., 2005; Nakahara et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of scientific knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Phosphorylated AID was reported to interact with Replication Protein A (RPA).
source: Phosphorylated AID was reported to interact with Replication Protein A (RPA), a protein also required for recombination, which then recruited AID to single-stranded DNA and facilitated the deamination of cytidines (Basu et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Basu et al., 2005.

claim: RPA recruited AID to single-stranded DNA and facilitated the deamination of cytidines.
source: Phosphorylated AID was reported to interact with Replication Protein A (RPA), a protein also required for recombination, which then recruited AID to single-stranded DNA and facilitated the deamination of cytidines (Basu et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Basu et al., 2005.

claim: RPA that accumulated at sites of AID-mediated DNA damage was shown to be associated with the RAD51 recombination protein.
source: The RPA that accumulated at sites of AID-mediated DNA damage was subsequently shown to be associated with the RAD51 recombination protein (Yamane et al., 2013), suggesting the formation of homologous recombination intermediates.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Yamane et al., 2013.

claim: The association of RPA with RAD51 at sites of AID-mediated DNA damage suggests the formation of homologous recombination intermediates.
source: The RPA that accumulated at sites of AID-mediated DNA damage was subsequently shown to be associated with the RAD51 recombination protein (Yamane et al., 2013), suggesting the formation of homologous recombination intermediates.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cited experimental observation.

claim: Inhibition of homologous recombination decreased the viability of B cells expressing AID and induced widespread double-strand breaks and genomic instability.
source: Notably, inhibition of homologous recombination decreased the viability of B cells expressing AID and induced widespread double-strand breaks and genomic instability (Hasham et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Hasham et al., 2010.

claim: The chicken B-cell line DT40 is easily modified by targeted gene integration.
source: The chicken B-cell line DT40, easily modified by targeted gene integration (Buerstedde and Takeda, 1991), is a useful model to study AID-mediated GC and SH (Di Noia and Neuberger, 2002; Arakawa and Buerstedde, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Buerstedde and Takeda, 1991.

claim: DT40 is a useful model to study AID-mediated gene conversion and somatic hypermutation.
source: The chicken B-cell line DT40, easily modified by targeted gene integration (Buerstedde and Takeda, 1991), is a useful model to study AID-mediated GC and SH (Di Noia and Neuberger, 2002; Arakawa and Buerstedde, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies using DT40 for these purposes.

claim: DT40 modifies its rearranged Ig light chain gene primarily by uni-directional gene conversion using nearby pseudo-V genes as conversion donor sequences.
source: DT40 modifies its rearranged Ig light chain gene primarily by uni-directional gene conversion using nearby pseudo-V genes as conversion donor sequences (Buerstedde et al., 1990).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Buerstedde et al., 1990.

claim: Gene conversion decreases and somatic hypermutation increases in DT40 if homologous recombination is impaired by inactivation of RAD51 paralogues.
source: However, GC decreases and SH increases if homologous recombination is impaired by inactivation of RAD51 paralogues (Sale et al., 2001), upon deletion of the upstream pseudo V genes that act as GC donor sequences (Arakawa et al., 2004) or following inactivation of the UNG gene (Saribasak et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Sale et al., 2001.

claim: Gene conversion decreases and somatic hypermutation increases in DT40 upon deletion of the upstream pseudo V genes that act as GC donor sequences.
source: However, GC decreases and SH increases if homologous recombination is impaired by inactivation of RAD51 paralogues (Sale et al., 2001), upon deletion of the upstream pseudo V genes that act as GC donor sequences (Arakawa et al., 2004) or following inactivation of the UNG gene (Saribasak et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Arakawa et al., 2004.

claim: Gene conversion decreases and somatic hypermutation increases in DT40 following inactivation of the UNG gene.
source: However, GC decreases and SH increases if homologous recombination is impaired by inactivation of RAD51 paralogues (Sale et al., 2001), upon deletion of the upstream pseudo V genes that act as GC donor sequences (Arakawa et al., 2004) or following inactivation of the UNG gene (Saribasak et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Saribasak et al., 2006.

claim: Somatic hypermutation of the Ig light chain gene and a GFP transgene were found to be strongly increased in the presence of a nearby Diversification Activator (DIVAC) sequence.
source: SH of the Ig light chain gene, as well as a green fluorescence protein (GFP) transgene were found to be strongly increased in the presence of a nearby Diversification Activator (DIVAC) sequence (Blagodatski et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Blagodatski et al., 2009.

claim: The DIVAC consists of the chicken enhancer and enhancer-like elements and can be replaced by the human Ig lambda and Ig heavy intron enhancers.
source: It was recently shown that this DIVAC consists of the chicken enhancer and enhancer-like elements and that it can be replaced by the human Ig lambda (hIgλE) and Ig heavy intron (IgHiE) enhancers (Buerstedde et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Buerstedde et al., 2014.

claim: CSR has been extensively studied using the murine B cell line CH12.
source: CSR has been extensively studied using the murine B cell line CH12 (Whitmore et al., 1991; Kinoshita et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies using CH12 cells.

claim: CH12 cells respond to appropriate stimulation by increasing both Ig switch region transcription and AID expression.
source: This model system responds to the appropriate stimulation by increasing both Ig switch region transcription and AID expression (Muramatsu et al., 2000) and by recombining its endogenous Ig heavy chain locus or transfected switch region constructs by CSR.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Muramatsu et al., 2000.

claim: CH12 cells recombine their endogenous Ig heavy chain locus or transfected switch region constructs by CSR upon stimulation.
source: This model system responds to the appropriate stimulation by increasing both Ig switch region transcription and AID expression (Muramatsu et al., 2000) and by recombining its endogenous Ig heavy chain locus or transfected switch region constructs by CSR.
evidence: This is established knowledge about CH12 cell behavior.

claim: AID has been known to induce homologous recombination in the form of unidirectional gene conversion.
source: While AID has been known to induce homologous recombination in the form of unidirectional gene conversion (Arakawa et al., 2002; Harris et al., 2002), there was previously no direct evidence that AID could mediate more complex rearrangements of sequence repeats.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Arakawa et al., 2002 and Harris et al., 2002.

claim: There was previously no direct evidence that AID could mediate more complex rearrangements of sequence repeats.
source: While AID has been known to induce homologous recombination in the form of unidirectional gene conversion (Arakawa et al., 2002; Harris et al., 2002), there was previously no direct evidence that AID could mediate more complex rearrangements of sequence repeats.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge prior to this study.

claim: AID can induce homologous recombination of repeats leading to frequent deletions between direct repeats in both DT40 and CH12 cells.
source: Using both DT40 and CH12 cells, we demonstrate here that AID can induce homologous recombination of repeats (RR) leading to frequent deletions between direct repeats.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Transfection of GFP-based hypermutation reporter constructs into DT40 suggested that in rare instances in which transgenes had undergone multi-copy integration there was frequent copy number contraction during cell clone expansion.
source: Transfection of GFP-based hypermutation reporter constructs into DT40 suggested that in rare instances in which transgenes had undergone multi-copy integration there was frequent copy number contraction during cell clone expansion (data not shown).
evidence: This is based on experimental observations from transfection experiments.

claim: Red fluorescence loss was stimulated 10- to 30-fold in the presence of the human Ig lambda enhancer (hIgλE) DIVAC.
source: Red fluorescence loss was stimulated 10- to 30-fold in the presence of the human Ig lambda enhancer (hIgλE) DIVAC (Buerstedde et al., 2014) (compare Figure 1B2 to Figure 1B3, Figure 1B4 to Figure 1B5; and Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1 and cited reference.

claim: Loss of red fluorescence was due to inactivation of the RFP transgenes by AID dependent, DIVAC-stimulated hypermutation events.
source: These results, combined with our previous extensive analyses of GFP-based reporter constructs (Blagodatski et al., 2009; Buerstedde et al., 2014), suggested that the loss of red fluorescence was due to inactivation of the RFP transgenes by AID dependent, DIVAC-stimulated hypermutation events.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental results and previous studies.

claim: A discrete cell population of intermediate red fluorescence was seen in transfectants of the tdT but not the DsR gene constructs.
source: Interestingly, a discrete cell population of intermediate red fluorescence was seen in transfectants of the tdT but not the DsR gene constructs (Figure 1B2 and Figure 1B3, circled).
evidence: This is shown in the FACS data in Figure 1.

claim: tdT is encoded by a direct tandem repeat of a RFP gene sequence.
source: Since tdT is encoded by a direct tandem repeat of a RFP gene sequence (Shaner et al., 2004), the intermediate red fluorescence possibly reflected the loss of one of the tdT repeats by intragenic recombination.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Shaner et al., 2004.

claim: The intermediate red fluorescence in tdT transfectants possibly reflected the loss of one of the tdT repeats by intragenic recombination.
source: Since tdT is encoded by a direct tandem repeat of a RFP gene sequence (Shaner et al., 2004), the intermediate red fluorescence possibly reflected the loss of one of the tdT repeats by intragenic recombination.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structure of tdT and the observed fluorescence pattern.

claim: Subclones of DIVAC_iHS_tdT_iHS transfectants showed green fluorescence positive, red fluorescence negative cells in the R1 gate at median frequencies of about 0.8%.
source: Subclones of transfectants showed, in addition to cells in the R3 gate (hereafter, R3 cells), green fluorescence positive, red fluorescence negative cells in the R1 gate at median frequencies of about 0.8% (Figure 2B2, Figure 2C).
evidence: This is shown in the experimental data in Figure 2.

claim: R1 cells are expected to arise if homologous recombination between the iHS sequences deleted the tdT gene and activated GFP translation due to the gain of the first ATG start codon previously located upstream of tdT.
source: Cells of this phenotype were expected to arise if homologous recombination between the iHS sequences deleted the tdT gene and activated GFP translation due to the gain of the first ATG start codon previously located upstream of tdT.
evidence: This is an inference based on the construct design and expected recombination outcomes.

claim: The appearance of R2 cells was strongly enhanced in the presence of either the hIgλE or hIgHiE DIVAC.
source: The appearance of these cells was strongly enhanced in the presence of either the hIgλE or hIgHiE DIVAC (compare Figure 2B4 to Figure 2B5,B7; and Figure 2C).
evidence: This is shown in the experimental data in Figure 2.

claim: Removal of the AID expression cassette from the DIVAC_iHS_tdT_iHS and DIVAC_RSV_tdT_RSV transfectants resulted in stable red fluorescence only expression.
source: Removal of the AID expression cassette from the DIVAC_iHS_tdT_iHS and DIVAC_RSV_tdT_RSV transfectants resulted in stable red fluorescence only expression (Figure 2B3, 2B6, Figure 2C) indicating that all fluorescence variation depended on AID.
evidence: This is shown in the experimental data in Figure 2.

claim: All fluorescence variation depended on AID.
source: Removal of the AID expression cassette from the DIVAC_iHS_tdT_iHS and DIVAC_RSV_tdT_RSV transfectants resulted in stable red fluorescence only expression (Figure 2B3, 2B6, Figure 2C) indicating that all fluorescence variation depended on AID.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental observation that removing AID stabilized fluorescence.

claim: The blasticidin resistance gene (bsr) would be lost if the iHS or the RSV promoter repeats of the dual fluorescence constructs underwent homologous recombination of repeats.
source: The blasticidin resistance gene (bsr), which is positioned between the RFP and GFP genes (Figure 2A), would be lost if the iHS or the RSV promoter repeats of the dual fluorescence constructs underwent homologous recombination of repeats (RR).
evidence: This is inferred from the construct design shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Addition of blasticidin to the culture eliminated R1 cells from the DIVAC_iHS_tdT_iHS transfectant and strongly reduced R2 cells of RSV repeat transfectants.
source: Addition of blasticidin to the culture indeed eliminated R1 cells from the DIVAC_iHS_tdT_iHS transfectant and strongly reduced R2 cells of RSV repeat transfectants (Figure 4A, compare upper to lower panel) consistent with the deletion of bsr in R1 and R2 cells.
evidence: This is shown in the experimental data in Figure 4A.

claim: R3 cells and cells of intermediate red fluorescence remained blasticidin resistant.
source: In contrast, R3 cells and cells of intermediate red fluorescence remained blasticidin resistant (Figure 4A, lower panel), as expected if these events reflected inactivation of the RFP gene by hypermutation and intragenic recombination of the tdT repeats, respectively.
evidence: This is shown in the experimental data in Figure 4A.

claim: R3 cells reflect inactivation of the RFP gene by hypermutation.
source: In contrast, R3 cells and cells of intermediate red fluorescence remained blasticidin resistant (Figure 4A, lower panel), as expected if these events reflected inactivation of the RFP gene by hypermutation and intragenic recombination of the tdT repeats, respectively.
evidence: This is inferred from the blasticidin resistance and the expected mechanism.

claim: Cells of intermediate red fluorescence reflect intragenic recombination of the tdT repeats.
source: In contrast, R3 cells and cells of intermediate red fluorescence remained blasticidin resistant (Figure 4A, lower panel), as expected if these events reflected inactivation of the RFP gene by hypermutation and intragenic recombination of the tdT repeats, respectively.
evidence: This is inferred from the blasticidin resistance and the expected mechanism.

claim: Subclones derived from cells showing altered fluorescence continued to generate variant cell populations during expansion.
source: Subclones derived from cells showing altered fluorescence continued to generate variant cell populations during expansion (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is shown in the experimental data in Figure 4B.

claim: PCR analysis showed that the intermediate red fluorescence subclone had deleted one of the tdT repeats.
source: Whereas the 1/3 primer pair amplified two fragments of about 1.7 kb and 2.5 kb from the primary transfectant (Figure 4C, lane 2 marked by asterisks), amplification from the intermediate red fluorescence subclone yielded only the lower fragment consistent with the deletion of one of the tdT repeats in cells of intermediate fluorescence (Figure 4C, lane 6).
evidence: This is shown in the PCR data in Figure 4C.

claim: PCR analysis of R2 subclones was consistent with a large deletion that included one RSV repeat and the intervening sequences.
source: The 1/2 and 1/3 primer pairs did not amplify the DNA of the R2 subclone (Figure 4C, lane 9 and 10) and the 1/4 and 1/5 primer pairs amplified only fragments of about 1.1 kb and 1.9 kb (Figure 4C, lane 11 and 12), but not the larger fragments of 4–5 kb size seen in addition to the lower size fragments in amplifications from the primary transfectant (Figure 4C, lane 3 and 4) and the intermediate red fluorescence subclone (Figure 4C, lanes 7 and 8). This was consistent with a large deletion that included one RSV repeat and the intervening sequences in R2 cells.
evidence: This is shown in the PCR data in Figure 4C and inferred from the fragment sizes.

claim: 12 sequences from sorted R2 cells showed deletions of one RSV repeat and the intervening sequence with no additional nucleotide changes.
source: The 1.9-kb fragment amplified by primer pair 1/5 from sorted DIVAC_RSV_tdT_RSV R2 cells was subcloned and sequenced. 12 sequences showed deletions of one RSV repeat and the intervening sequence with no additional nucleotide changes when compared to the sequence of the transfected construct (data not shown).
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis of PCR products.

claim: AID induces intragenic homologous recombination between the tdT repeats and intergenic recombination between the RSV promoter sequences at high frequencies.
source: These analyses demonstrate that AID induces intragenic homologous recombination between the tdT repeats and intergenic recombination between the RSV promoter sequences at high frequencies.
evidence: This is concluded from the PCR and sequence analysis data.

claim: The median percentage of R1 and R2 events was lower in DIVAC_uHS_tdT_dHS transfectants, most likely due to inhibition of homologous recombination by the heterologies of the uHS/dHS sequences.
source: The median percentage of R1 and R2 events was lower, however (Figure 5B,C), most likely due to inhibition of homologous recombination by the heterologies of the uHS/dHS sequences.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data in Figure 5 and the known effect of sequence heterology on recombination.

claim: Only subclones derived from R1- and R2-gated cells were killed upon addition of blasticidin, indicating that these cells but not the cells in other gates had deleted the bsr gene.
source: Only subclones derived from R1- and R2-gated cells were killed upon addition of blasticidin, indicating that these cells but not the cells in other gates had deleted the bsr gene (data not shown).
evidence: This is based on experimental observation of blasticidin sensitivity.

claim: PCR analysis showed that R1 and R2 cells had recombined uHS/dHS, and R4 cells had recombined the tdT repeat, whereas R3, R5, R6 cells did not carry detectable rearrangements.
source: This indicated that R1 and R2 cells had recombined uHS/dHS, and R4 cells had recombined the tdT repeat, whereas R3, R5, R6 cells did not carry detectable rearrangements.
evidence: This is concluded from the PCR analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Analysis of recombined sequences amplified from gated R1 and R2 cells provided evidence for variable crossover positions.
source: Analysis of recombined sequences amplified by the 1/5 primer pair from gated R1 and R2 cells indeed provided evidence for variable crossover positions (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is shown in the sequence analysis data in Figure 7B.

claim: All R1 sequences had maintained uHS-specific sequence at least until the single nucleotide insertion polymorphism that puts the upstream ATG codon in frame with tdT prior to recombination and in frame with GFP after recombination.
source: All R1 sequences had maintained uHS-specific sequence at least until the single nucleotide insertion polymorphism (marked by two vertical arrows in Figure 7A) that puts the upstream ATG codon in frame with tdT prior to recombination and in frame with GFP after recombination.
evidence: This is shown in the sequence analysis data in Figure 7.

claim: The maintenance of uHS-specific sequence until the critical insertion polymorphism explains the strong increase in green fluorescence seen in R1 cells.
source: This explains the strong increase in green fluorescence seen in R1 cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the sequence analysis and the effect on GFP translation.

claim: All R2 sequences maintained dHS-specific sequence at the critical insertion polymorphism position.
source: In contrast, all R2 sequences maintained dHS-specific sequence at this position (Figure 7B) suggesting again that modest increase of green fluorescence in R2 cells is either due to enhanced GFP transcription or the gain of an alternative GFP translation start codon.
evidence: This is shown in the sequence analysis data in Figure 7B.

claim: Five R1 sequences maintained uHS sequence down to the last polymorphic nucleotide in front of the GFP reading frame and five R2 sequences maintained dHS sequence up to the last polymorphic nucleotide downstream of the hIgλE sequence, suggesting preferential crossover events near the boundaries of sequence homology.
source: Five R1 sequences (S1, S2, S3, S4, and S7) maintained uHS sequence down to the last polymorphic nucleotide in front of the GFP reading frame and five R2 sequences (S14, S20, S23, S26, S30) maintained dHS sequence up to the last polymorphic nucleotide downstream of the hIgλE sequence, suggesting preferential crossover events near the boundaries of sequence homology.
evidence: This is inferred from the sequence analysis data.

claim: Six sequences from R2 cells contained either single or multiple dHS-specific nucleotides upstream of uHS-specific nucleotides, most easily explained by mismatch repair of recombination associated heteroduplexes.
source: Interestingly, six sequences from R2 cells (S9, S10, S12, S13, S18, S21) contained either single or multiple dHS-specific nucleotides upstream of uHS-specific nucleotides (marked by red circles in these sequence in Figure 7B), most easily explained by mismatch repair of recombination associated heteroduplexes.
evidence: This is inferred from the sequence patterns observed in Figure 7B.

claim: Four sequences amplified from gated R4 cells showed deletion of one tdT repeat and the 69-bp intervening sequence between tdT repeats with no other sequence changes confirming that cells of intermediate red fluorescence were due to intragenic tdT repeat recombination.
source: Four sequences amplified from gated R4 cells by the 1/3 primer pair showed deletion of one tdT repeat and the 69-bp intervening sequence between tdT repeats with no other sequence changes confirming that cells of intermediate red fluorescence were due to intragenic tdT repeat recombination (data not shown).
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis of PCR products from R4 cells.

claim: Two uHS sequences amplified from R5 subclones showed that the middle part had converted to dHS-specific sequence thereby erasing the first ATG start codon.
source: Two uHS sequences amplified by the 1/3 primer pair from R5 subclones showed that the middle part had converted to dHS-specific sequence thereby erasing the first ATG start codon (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is shown in the sequence analysis data in Figure 7C.

claim: If the canonical tdT protein translated from the second ATG codon were more active than the artificial tdT fusion protein translated from the first ATG codon, this would explain the increased red fluorescence of R5 cells.
source: If the canonical tdT protein translated from the second ATG codon were more active than the artificial tdT fusion protein translated from the first ATG codon, this would explain the increased red fluorescence of R5 cells.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed phenotype.

claim: The observed sequence changes in R5 cells likely reflected unidirectional dHS-templated gene conversions.
source: The observed sequence changes likely reflected unidirectional dHS-templated gene conversions, as an increase of green fluorescence was not observed in R5 cells, but would have been expected if a reciprocal exchange had introduced the first ATG codon into dHS.
evidence: This is inferred from the sequence changes and the absence of green fluorescence increase.

claim: dHS sequences amplified from an R6 subclone showed the insertion of seven uHS specific nucleotides including the downstream ATG start codon upstream of the GFP coding sequence.
source: Surprisingly, dHS sequences amplified from an R6 subclone (with very high green fluorescence) by the 1/5 primer pair showed the insertion of seven uHS specific nucleotides including the downstream ATG start codon upstream of the GFP coding sequence (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is shown in the sequence analysis data in Figure 7D.

claim: The sequence change in R6 cells explaining the strongly increased green fluorescence was most likely enabled by a stretch of 12 identical nucleotides at the beginning of the tdT and GFP coding sequences.
source: This change—explaining the strongly increased green fluorescence of R6 cells—was most likely enabled by a stretch of 12 identical nucleotides at the beginning of the tdT and GFP coding sequences.
evidence: This is inferred from the sequence analysis and the construct design.

claim: The appearance of R5 cells can be explained by dHS-templated gene conversion leading to the loss of the first ATG codon in uHS.
source: These results show that the appearance of R5 cells can be explained by dHS-templated gene conversion leading to the loss of the first ATG codon in uHS whereas the appearance of R6 cells reflect uHS-templated gene conversion leading to the gain of the second ATG codon at the very end of dHS.
evidence: This is concluded from the sequence analysis data.

claim: The appearance of R6 cells reflects uHS-templated gene conversion leading to the gain of the second ATG codon at the very end of dHS.
source: These results show that the appearance of R5 cells can be explained by dHS-templated gene conversion leading to the loss of the first ATG codon in uHS whereas the appearance of R6 cells reflect uHS-templated gene conversion leading to the gain of the second ATG codon at the very end of dHS.
evidence: This is concluded from the sequence analysis data.

claim: Gene conversions within the uHS/dHS repeat occurred about 3–10 times less frequently than deletions by RR.
source: Gene conversions within the uHS/dHS repeat occurred about 3–10 times less frequently than deletions by RR, based on the analysis of subclones of three independent DIVAC_uHS_tdT_dHS transfectants (compare the medians of R1 and R2 vs R5 and R6 events in Figure 5C).
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of the frequencies shown in Figure 5C.

claim: When DIVAC_RSV_Sμ_tdT_RSV_Sα was introduced into DT40 by targeted integration, transfectants accumulated cells in the R1 and R2 gates at median frequencies of about 0.15% and 5% respectively after 12 days culture.
source: When DIVAC_RSV_Sμ_tdT_RSV_Sα was introduced into DT40 by targeted integration, transfectants accumulated cells in the R1 and R2 gates at median frequencies of about 0.15% and 5% respectively after 12 days culture (Figure 8B1 and data not shown).
evidence: This is shown in the experimental data in Figure 8B1.

claim: The frequency at which R1 and R2 cells were generated was strongly increased when factors known to increase both AID expression and Ig CSR were added to the culture of CH12 transfectants.
source: The frequency at which R1 and R2 cells were generated was strongly increased when factors known to increase both AID expression and Ig CSR (Kinoshita et al., 1998) were added to the culture of CH12 transfectants (compare Figure 8B2 to Figure 8B3 and data not shown).
evidence: This is shown in the experimental data in Figure 8B and supported by citation.

claim: The DT40 transfectant showed about 50 times fewer R1 than R2 cells.
source: Whereas the DT40 transfectant showed about 50 times fewer R1 than R2 cells, the frequency of cells in the two gates was roughly equal in CH12 transfectants indicating increased CSR in CH12 as compared to DT40 cells.
evidence: This is based on quantitative comparison of the FACS data.

claim: The frequency of cells in the R1 and R2 gates was roughly equal in CH12 transfectants indicating increased CSR in CH12 as compared to DT40 cells.
source: Whereas the DT40 transfectant showed about 50 times fewer R1 than R2 cells, the frequency of cells in the two gates was roughly equal in CH12 transfectants indicating increased CSR in CH12 as compared to DT40 cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the quantitative comparison of R1 and R2 frequencies.

claim: Amplification from DT40 R1 and CH12 R1 cells produced a smear of fragments in the range of about 2.5–3.2 kb as expected for diverse switch region recombination events.
source: Amplification from DT40 R1 (Figure 8D, lane 1) and CH12 R1 (Figure 8D, lane 3) cells produced a smear of fragments in the range of about 2.5–3.2 kb as expected for diverse switch region recombination events.
evidence: This is shown in the PCR data in Figure 8D.

claim: A discrete fragment of about 3.1 kb was amplified from CH12 R2 cells as expected for RSV repeat recombination.
source: In contrast, a discrete fragment of about 3.1 kb was amplified from CH12 R2 cells (Figure 8D, lane 4) and to a lesser degree from CH12 unsorted cells (Figure 8D, lane 2) as expected for RSV repeat recombination.
evidence: This is shown in the PCR data in Figure 8D.

claim: Sequences from both DT40 and CH12 cells had joined the upstream Sμ to downstream Sα switch regions at variable positions displaying unusually long junctional microhomologies.
source: Sequences from both DT40 and CH12 cells had joined the upstream Sμ to downstream Sα switch regions at variable positions displaying unusually long junctional microhomologies (Figure 9A,B) similar to recombination events previously reported using similar constructs (Kinoshita et al., 1998; Okazaki et al., 2002).
evidence: This is shown in the sequence analysis data in Figure 9 and compared to cited studies.

claim: Ten sequences from sorted CH12 R2 DNA showed uniform deletions of one RSV repeat and the intervening sequence with no other sequence changes as expected for faithful RR events.
source: To confirm recombination of RSV repeats in CH12 cells, we subcloned and sequenced the 3.1 kb band amplified from sorted CH12 R2 DNA. Ten sequences showed uniform deletions of one RSV repeat and the intervening sequence with no other sequence changes as expected for faithful RR events.
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis of PCR products.

claim: DT40 and CH12 cells carried out both RSV and switch region recombination, but the absolute and relative frequencies of switch recombination were about 5 and 30-fold higher, respectively, in induced CH12 cells.
source: These results demonstrate that DT40 and CH12 cells carried out both RSV and switch region recombination, but the absolute and relative frequencies of switch recombination were about 5 and 30-fold higher, respectively, in induced CH12 cells.
evidence: This is concluded from the quantitative analysis of the experimental data.

claim: The finding that AID can induce chromosomal deletions by homologous recombination of repeats adds another activity to the remarkable array of AID-induced mutation and recombination events.
source: The finding that AID can induce chromosomal deletions by homologous recombination of repeats (RR) adds another activity to the remarkable array of AID-induced mutation and recombination events.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main finding.

claim: Transfectants of DT40 recombined the duplicated RSV promoters and tdT repeats as frequently by RR as they inactivated the RFP genes by somatic hypermutation.
source: Interestingly, transfectants of DT40 recombined the duplicated RSV promoters and tdT repeats as frequently by RR as they inactivated the RFP genes by somatic hypermutation (SH).
evidence: This is based on comparison of frequencies from the experimental data.

claim: An artificial homeologous sequence upstream of the tdT and GFP genes was recombined more often by RR than it was modified by GC in DT40.
source: Although DT40 diversifies its Ig genes by gene conversion (GC), an artificial homeologous sequence upstream of the tdT and GFP genes was recombined more often by RR than it was modified by GC.
evidence: This is based on comparison of frequencies from the experimental data.

claim: Class switch recombination active CH12 cells rearranged a construct containing duplicated RSV promoters and intronic switch regions as often by RR as by CSR.
source: Similarly, class switch recombination (CSR) active CH12 cells rearranged a construct containing duplicated RSV promoters and intronic switch regions as often by RR as by CSR.
evidence: This is based on comparison of frequencies from the experimental data.

claim: AID-induced RR does not seem to involve error prone DNA synthesis because precise deletions, but no non-templated nucleotide changes, were encountered in a large number of recombinant sequences.
source: AID-induced RR does not seem to involve error prone DNA synthesis because precise deletions, but no non-templated nucleotide changes, were encountered in a large number of recombinant sequences.
evidence: This is inferred from the sequence analysis showing only precise deletions.

claim: The single strand nick believed to occur after the excision of an AID-induced uracil is further processed into a homologous recombination intermediate.
source: To explain RR, we propose that the single strand nick—believed to occur after the excision of an AID-induced uracil (Figure 10B)—is further processed into a homologous recombination intermediate.
evidence: This is a proposed model to explain the observed RR.

claim: The homologous recombination intermediate could either be a single strand gap generated by nuclease mediated resection of the nicked strand or a double strand break from replication fork collapse.
source: This could either be a single strand gap generated by nuclease mediated resection of the nicked strand (Model 1, Figure 10C–F) or a double strand break believed to occur when the replication fork collapses at the site of the unrepaired single strand nick within one of the template strands (Kowalczykowski, 2000; Petermann and Helleday, 2010) (Model 2, Figure 10G–K).
evidence: This is a proposed model supported by citations to relevant literature.

claim: Both models invoke substantial DNA resection to expose single stranded DNA distant from the nicks.
source: Since recombination occurred at high frequency between the RSV repeats, which are upstream of the transcription start site and hence likely to be hundreds of bases away from the peak of AID-induced cytidine deamination (Saribasak et al., 2006), both models invoke substantial DNA resection to expose single stranded DNA distant from the nicks (Figure 10C,I).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of recombination at distant sites and supported by citation.

claim: The fact that RPA accumulated at multiple chromosomal positions within activated murine B cells in an AID-dependent fashion is consistent with the formation of recombination competent nucleoprotein filaments.
source: The fact that RPA (Hakim et al., 2012) as well as RPA together with RAD51 (Yamane et al., 2013) accumulated at multiple chromosomal positions within activated murine B cells in an AID-dependent fashion is consistent with the formation of recombination competent nucleoprotein filaments.
evidence: This is inferred from cited studies showing RPA and RAD51 accumulation.

claim: RR could be responsible for V gene replacements that are not associated with cryptic V(D)J signal recognition sequences, as these were observed in AID expressing germinal center B cells.
source: For example, it could be responsible for V gene replacements that are not associated with cryptic V(D)J signal recognition sequences, as these were observed in AID expressing germinal center B cells (Darlow and Stott, 2005).
evidence: This is a speculative connection to observed phenomena supported by citation.

claim: Gene conversion and RR might involve the same intermediates leading to sequence alignment and strand invasion and later diverge when the Holliday junctions are resolved by cleavage during RR, but by convergent branch migration during GC.
source: Intriguingly, the two processes might involve the same intermediates leading to sequence alignment and strand invasion (Figure 10C,D) and later diverge when the Holliday junctions (Figure 10E) are resolved by cleavage during RR, but by convergent branch migration during GC.
evidence: This is a speculative model for the relationship between GC and RR.

claim: RR is likely to add to the mutation signature of AID by introducing deletions and inversions of repetitive sequences.
source: While possibly involved in the repair of AID-induced DNA damage, RR is also likely to add to the mutation signature of AID by introducing deletions and inversions of repetitive sequences.
evidence: This is inferred from the demonstrated RR activity of AID.

claim: AID expressing B cells are prone to transformation.
source: AID expressing B cells are prone to transformation (Robbiani and Nussenzweig, 2013) and mutation signatures of APOBEC homologues are found in the genomes of many cancer cells (Alexandrov et al., 2013; Burns et al., 2013; Taylor et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Robbiani and Nussenzweig, 2013.

claim: Mutation signatures of APOBEC homologues are found in the genomes of many cancer cells.
source: AID expressing B cells are prone to transformation (Robbiani and Nussenzweig, 2013) and mutation signatures of APOBEC homologues are found in the genomes of many cancer cells (Alexandrov et al., 2013; Burns et al., 2013; Taylor et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Cis-acting sequences that activate SH in nearby transcribed sequences (DIVACs) strongly stimulated the frequency of RR.
source: Cis-acting sequences that activate SH in nearby transcribed sequences and which have been termed DIVersification ACtivators (DIVACs) (Buerstedde et al., 2014), strongly stimulated the frequency of RR, revealing an additional risk to genome integrity posed by DIVAC-like sequences outside of the Ig loci.
evidence: This is based on experimental data showing increased RR with DIVACs.

claim: DIVACs reveal an additional risk to genome integrity posed by DIVAC-like sequences outside of the Ig loci.
source: Cis-acting sequences that activate SH in nearby transcribed sequences and which have been termed DIVersification ACtivators (DIVACs) (Buerstedde et al., 2014), strongly stimulated the frequency of RR, revealing an additional risk to genome integrity posed by DIVAC-like sequences outside of the Ig loci.
evidence: This is inferred from the stimulation of RR by DIVACs.

claim: RR-mediated deletions were detectable after transfection of 'no DIVAC' containing control constructs.
source: However, RR-mediated deletions were also detectable after transfection of 'no DIVAC' containing control constructs (e.g., R2 events arising from the RSV_tdT_RSV substrate; Figure 2B,C).
evidence: This is shown in the experimental data in Figure 2.

claim: AID and perhaps other cytidine deaminases represent a general threat to transcribed regions of the genome via multiple mechanisms including RR.
source: Thus, AID and perhaps other cytidine deaminases represent a general threat to transcribed regions of the genome via multiple mechanisms including RR, as reported here.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the findings of the study.

claim: Given the highly repetitive nature of mammalian genomes, even a low level of RR could significantly contribute to genome instability and B cell transformation.
source: Given the highly repetitive nature of mammalian genomes, even a low level of RR could significantly contribute to genome instability and B cell transformation.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential impact of RR.
